item.title: Do We Still Need Mathematicians?
item.dc:creator: Bennie Mols
item.description: “We’re going to get superhuman mathematicians very soon, and mathematics itself will be pushed forward.”
item.content:encoded:
When OpenAI claimed on September 8, 2026, that an internal AI system had produced a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, it sent shock waves through the mathematical community and far beyond it. Scientific American first ran an article under the headline “The summer AI ate math,” but later changed it to the still rather hyperbolic “If AI can do math, what’s the point of mathematicians?”

The Heidelberg Laureate Forum’s panel discussion “AI in Mathematical Research,” held one week later, could not have come at a better time. Moderated by mathematician Tony Feng of the University of California, Berkeley, the panel brought together Fields Medalists Peter Scholze of Germany’s Max Planck Institute for Mathematics and Jacob Tsimerman of Canada’s University of Toronto, as well as  Geordie Williamson of Australia’s University of Sydney, a pioneer in applying AI to mathematical research, and Michael Harris of Columbia University, a prominent number theorist.

Asked how much time they each had spent talking to AI during the previous week, Harris and Scholze both answered: zero. “I’ve never typed anything into a large language model,” Scholze said, adding, “I’m living in a small AI-free bubble, but it’s about to burst, I think.” Williamson estimated his AI-for-math use at three or four hours a day, sometimes leaving AI systems running overnight. Tsimerman said his AI use for math was limited to 30 minutes to an hour a day, which he called “a low week.”

For Tsimerman, who recently joined OpenAI to work on AI safety, AI has become something like a research collaborator. His use has evolved from searching the literature and checking ideas in fields in which he is not an expert, to directing coding agents and sub-agents to explore different approaches. “I would essentially prompt the coding agent with: ‘I think something like this should work. Please spawn several sub-agents: you try this method, you try that method, report back, write a report to me’.”            

Tsimerman expects much more to come. “We’re going to get superhuman mathematicians very soon, and mathematics itself will be pushed forward.” Problems that today lie beyond the reach of human researchers may suddenly become accessible as mathematics begins to move “at a superhuman rate,” he said. Rather than fearing that acceleration, he said mathematicians should prepare for this radically new reality.

Scholze questioned the premise that faster mathematics is necessarily better. He compared the seven Millennium Prize Problems to “mountains far out in the mathematical landscape, where we don’t even know the landscape around them.” Their real purpose, he argued, is “to illuminate that landscape, not so much to solve the specific problem.”

The real bottleneck in mathematical research, said Scholze, is not the production of new results, but the ability of mathematicians to develop a shared human understanding of them. “AI wants to accelerate everything, and I don’t see any inherent value in acceleration itself,” he said. “If results accelerate further, there’s just less human understanding.”

Williamson is much more enthusiastic about using AI, but said he sees a related problem. For a long time, solving difficult problems served as a reasonable proxy for mathematical understanding and contribution to the community. AI may now be breaking that link. “Now our community has the challenge to reevaluate how we assess people, who gets jobs, how we educate people et cetera.”

Harris was by far the most critical of the panelists, particularly of commercial AI. He said he refuses to use commercial LLMs, which he sees as appropriating publicly shared intellectual work for private profit. Mathematics has always functioned as a gift economy, he said: researchers freely build on one another’s work as part of a shared intellectual culture.

“The vision of a Humboldtian university,” said Harris, “where the principles are independence from external interference and from subordination to short-term economic considerations, is under attack, specifically from ideologues in Silicon Valley.” In that spirit, he endorses the Leiden Declaration published in June for, among other things, university-based laboratories for automated mathematics.

Some younger mathematicians already are organizing around similar concerns. Students and postdocs recently founded the Association for Human Mathematics. Members pledge either not to work with commercial AI labs and not to use AI to write papers or, more strongly, not to use AI at all. Harris called this “an expression of confidence in human imagination that should be recognized and applauded.”

Tsimerman, however, noted a lack of urgency in the mathematical community. “The world in two years is going to look so incredibly different than it does now,” he said.

Yet predicting superhuman mathematical AI, he stressed, is not the same as declaring human mathematics obsolete. “There’s a big difference between ‘there’s not going to be forefront theorems proven by human mathematicians,’ which is something that I believe is going to be true very soon, and ‘there’s no place for human mathematics,’ which I very much don’t believe.”

Human engagement with mathematics, Tsimerman said, remains valuable as part of human culture. And because AI systems can be unreliable or unaligned with human values, human expertise remains essential: “It’s very hard to have oversight if you don’t have expertise,” he said.

For Williamson, the impact of AI extends far beyond mathematics. “Do we want to construct a world in which human understanding plays no role?” he asked. “I think that I don’t.” Mathematics, he suggested, seems an early test case for what is about to happen across all intellectual work. AI may add a new style of doing mathematics without making the traditional one superfluous. Scholze clearly prefers the traditional style. Calling himself “a dinosaur,” he said he does not even like to sit in front of a computer and type. “I like to think about mathematics on my own, just wander around, talk to others.”

Williamson enjoys using AI to explore new territory. “One of the many things that I adore about mathematics is just the surprise,” he said. “Some problem that you have been working on for some time is solved by a colleague, and the solution is really surprising. And I’ve had a couple of experiences now with AI where it suggests something about a problem that is really surprising, and I love that.”

Bennie Mols is a science and technology writer based in Amsterdam, the Netherlands.

item.title: The Next Frontier in AI-Enabled Coding: Scaling Development
item.dc:creator: Amy Buttell
item.description: Developers, teams, and organizations are identifying solutions to streamline the AI-enabled coding process and accelerate development and product shipment.
item.content:encoded:
There’s little doubt AI-enabled coding tools can expedite the first part of the coding process: writing code. However, bottlenecks appear once the code is written, which call into question whether AI-enabled coding genuinely improves the speed at which development takes place and products ship.

CircleCI’s 2026 State of Software Delivery documents the costs: while more code is being written, the rate at which development is finished and released fell at the same time during their study, which occurred between Sept. 1 to Sept. 28, 2025.1 AI-enabled code tends to fail at higher rates and takes longer to fix, which leads to more developer time lost, fewer products shipping, and questionable AI investment ROI.1

The next frontier in AI-enabled development seeks to harness the power of LLM-based AI coding platforms to scale coding and development to speed products (codes and programs) to market. Because LLM platforms develop and release new versions rapidly, defining the challenges involved in AI-enabled coding is a moving target.

“The bottleneck is both a process problem and an understanding problem,” said Margaret-Anne Storey, professor of computer science at Canada’s University of Victoria. “Understanding now needs to be a deliverable. We always thought of code as the deliverable when humans were writing code because you would write the code, your program would execute, and your understanding was recoverable from the code. Now, AI writes the code, so what we need to do is think about the architecture, which influences product security, performance, integration, and evolution.”

As understanding evolves, developers, teams, and organizations are identifying solutions to streamline the AI-enabled coding process and accelerate development and product shipment.

Challenges to Scaling AI-Enabled Coding

AI-enabled coding, whether directly through AI coding assistants or through AI agents, creates three specific types of debt that then cascade into a variety of concrete challenges that developers, teams, and organizations encounter as they seek to accelerate development and product shipment.

Storey originated the triple-debt concept around software health, which she explained in a paper published in ACM Queue: “Technical debt refers to problems in the code layer, cognitive debt refers to erosion of the shared understanding across a team over time, and intent debt refers to a lack of externalized goals, constraints, and rationale that both humans and AI systems need to work safely and efficiently within a codebase.”2

“Technical debt makes systems harder to change,” she continued in the paper. “Cognitive debt makes systems harder to understand. Intent debt makes it difficult to know what the system is actually for.”2

For Nik Kale, principal engineer at networking company and contributor to the Coalition for Secure AI, AI coding must reduce the total effort required to deliver a dependable change to create value. “More AI in the building still means more change failures and more recovery work even after raw speed recovers,” he said.

“DORA’s 2026 report names the mechanism and calls it the verification tax, the added effort of checking whether generated code is correct, secure, and architecturally coherent,” Kale added. “Writing code was never really the bottleneck and rather was just the only part of the lifecycle anyone had bothered to instrument.”

Solutions to Scaling AI-Enabled Coding

Because LLM models are evolving rapidly, the solutions to scaling AI-enabled coding are in flux. At the same time, developers, teams, and organizations are starting to figure out the investment, processes, and procedures to implement to streamline AI coding, avoid or overcome bottlenecks, and expedite the entire process to accelerate product development. Several solutions are available.

Treating AI as an internal product or service: “With the tools and investment, what’s going to be really potent in the next two to three years is the fact of treating how you are implementing AI as an internal product or service,” said David Longnecker, an AI and technology consultant. “Just like building up a team wiki in Sharepoint, an organizational AI tool is something that will have to be owned and maintained with observability and explainability behind it.”

Longnecker described AI as “an internal service we provide,” explaining, “Here is the team that are the service providers in charge of rolling out standard operating procedures, teaching people who are using the tool independently to use it in the same direction. It’s going to require investment not just in technology, but in people. You can’t fire all the people because AI is going to do all the things; you’re going to have to hire them back to keep the AI in line.”

Employing context engineering: Context engineering relates to managing the context developers give AI agents, according to Storey. “Context engineering involves thinking about the kind of information that we should give to our AI coding agents,” she said. “Sometimes it’s called a constitution; like a constitution for the agents, the advice that they need to do a task correctly.”

Creating or using an agentic AI development platform: IBM launched an agentic AI development platform called Bob in April 2026 to automate the software development lifecycle. Instead of responding to isolated prompts, Bob coordinates specialized AI agents across roles and lifecycle stages.3 IBM uses Bob internally and makes Bob available to clients as an SaaS offering.

“Bob supports models that mimic different roles, rules that help create standardized templates, skills that help author playbooks, and tools that enable automation and gates for checkpointing,” said Neel Sundaresan, general manager of automation and AI at IBM. “These capabilities help create artifacts specific to individual states of the software development lifecycle, where Bob can assist, augment, or automate the work of a human in that role.”

Sundaresan noted that beyond efficiency, Bob streamlines the team dynamic, which allows development teams to align faster, iterate with confidence, and bring higher quality products to market.

Building automation to support and distribute code review: “We use LLMs to review code at four levels—commit, pull request, feature, and release—classifying findings according to internal definitions between must-fix and nice-to-fix,” said Breno Oliveira, chief technology officer at Strider, a platform for hiring and retaining remote developers. “We’ve also built automations that distribute code reviews more effectively, ensuring a balanced workload but also driving improved accuracy by ensuring, for example, that the reviewer is familiar with a feature or the code involved.”

References

1. Powell, R., and Schmitt, J. The New Reality of Software Delivery. CircleCI; https://circleci.com/resources/2026-state-of-software-delivery/

2. Storey, M-A. From Technical Debt to Cognitive and Intent Debt: Rethinking Software Health in the Age of AI. ACM Queue; https://queue.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3807966

3. Introducing IBM Bob: AI Development Partner that Takes Enterprises from AI-Assisted Coding to Production-Ready Software. IBM; https://bit.ly/48j2ZfB

Amy Buttell is a Silver Spring, MD-based technology, legal, and business journalist, content creator, writer, and ghostwriter.

item.title: When You Wish Upon a Prompt
item.dc:creator: George V. Neville-Neil
item.description: The key skills in software are the skills of software engineering, writ large.
item.content:encoded:
Dear KV,

I have noticed in your recent columns that, like everyone else, you are writing about LLMs and their effect on the practice of programming. As academics who have to teach the next generation of practitioners how to practice, my colleagues and I now find ourselves in the unenviable position of having to go back to the drawing board and work out ways to inculcate the necessary skills while competing with systems that help students complete tasks in considerably less time and with considerably less mental effort. It is well understood that mental effort is required to learn a topic, which is why writing notes by hand continues to result in better learning outcomes than typing them on a laptop or, even worse, absorbing a video lecture.

Since you are an older practitioner who is seeing this transition from the other side, what do you think those of us who are training your replacements should be teaching? Or is it time to let the machines do the work and just give our students our best wishes?

If Wishes Were Horses

Dear Wishes,

It is true that Kode Vicious, like many others in the industry, has been writing about, and more generally dealing with, the LLM craze/fad/bubble—pick a term here. As we have progressed through the past two or so years of this craze, I will call it, the thing that has struck me most is not the increase in our ability to produce more reams of code, but all the hand-wringing on all sides of, “Oh what do we do? What do we do?”

The key skills in software are not typing speed or the visual acuity to spot a missing dereference, but instead they are the skills of software engineering, writ large. What are these skills? They are the ones we were all supposed to be learning, during that one software engineering course everyone was required to take. As KV wrote eons ago, the best thing I ever got out of a software engineering course was reading the Mythical Man-Month by Fred Brooks, and while that book is a deserved classic, it is more about management than about the proper engineering of software artifacts.

While most computing degrees during the past 50 or more years have concentrated on teaching specific technologies (programming in Fortran, or C, or Python, with a side of data structures) or instead went in the other direction into the aerie ether of functional languages and closures, very little time was spent on teaching people how to think about systems.

Now I know that everyone is surprised that KV can be a pedant, but let’s start with the basics. A program is a set of instructions to the computer that get the hardware to do something—hopefully something productive, but at least something. The best programs are made up of libraries, smaller pieces of code that tell the computer to do a more narrowly defined thing. Code, in all its forms, describes algorithms, abstract concepts of how a computer can do a thing. Programs are written in languages that are, supposedly, better at representing the ideas of their human creators than, say, machine code. The keys to making a good software system do not lie in the language specifics or its syntax, although one can make some truly dreadful messes of both, but rather in how the system is put together.

The keys to good software engineering are the interfaces between components, the testability of those components, both for correctness and performance, and how the whole system works together to yield something that is both usable and maintainable over the long term. These are the skills that software engineers need to be trained in—not being able to scan 100 lines of code for a missing asterisk. The computer can do that, and now even faster with the help of LLMs.

When compilers first started replacing assemblers and machine code, they allowed for new levels of abstraction. And it is this topic, abstraction, that we must continue to teach, because it is at the heart of maintainable systems. With the current LLMs, anyone can generate a working program based on a wish—that is, if they wish hard enough (that is, they prompt a lot). But a program is not a system, and the only people KV has seen be successful with these new tools are those who already have the software engineering discipline to know the difference between a program and a system.

How would KV teach such topics? The first thing academia will have to do is to dedicate a lot more time to mentoring interaction, perhaps through teaching assistants who take the time to probe the designs the students show to them. It’s pretty clear that most current programming projects can be solved by the best LLMs without much work from the students. But if you ask the student, “How does it work?”, you will find they often do not know. Finding ways to get them to the point where they can explain how it works is key to training the next group of practitioners.

KV was lucky enough to go to high school in a state that required lab reports for all science courses (biology, chemistry, and physics). Once a week we did an experiment and then had to write it up in a typical “Hypothesis, Experimental Design, Measurements, Evaluation, Conclusions” format. For computer science students, you might just give them the whole program and a set of inputs and ask, “Why?” Now, can an LLM answer this as well? Yes, for simple systems, but it turns out that someone with experience can probe and ask questions the student failed to ask of the LLM since the student does not even know to ask them. A few rounds of this will teach the student what is and is not important in understanding a system—far more than making them implement bubble sort ever would.

Implementing bubble sort does not teach you about when or why to use it, or what the proper interfaces to such an algorithm might be. Questions about sorting algorithms, given the same inputs, and then asking the student to explain why you choose one over the other will actually teach them about algorithmic complexity, performance, and proper APIs.

One of the great teaching advances that is not used often enough is the gigantic corpus of open source software that exists in the world today. It is far more educational to give students a large working system and have them debug it than it is to see if they can each, individually or in pairs, write a sorting algorithm (or whatever other piece of code you would expect a first-year student to crank out over a week or two).

Newly minted practitioners will need a skill that many of us developed naturally, which is to know when the computer is wrong. And this is even more true when using LLMs. People say, “The LLMs lie,” or they “hallucinate,” even though anthropomorphizing computers does not help at all.

The ability to separate the wheat from the chaff is something every software engineer has had to learn how to do, more often on the job than in school. The wheat and the chaff used to come from other programmers. Now it also comes from the computer itself, but the mental skills to deal with it are the same as they ever were. It comes down to knowing how a system looks when it is properly put together. Teach these skills and you, as well as those of us who live long enough to use systems coded by these students, will be grateful. Teach them to spot an errant asterisk, however, and we are all going to be very, very unhappy.

KV
